back: A material whose properties change in a controlled, usually reversible way in response to a stimulus such as heat, light, pressure, moisture or electricity.
A material developed through new or improved processes to give properties traditional materials cannot.
Change colour in UV light and reverse when it is removed — self-darkening lenses, UV security inks.
Change colour with temperature — baby spoons, mugs, battery test strips, food packaging.
Tiny droplets trapped in a coating that bursts when rubbed, pressed or heated — scratch-and-sniff, fragranced textiles.
A metal alloy that can be deformed when cool and returns to its pre-set shape when heated.
An alloy of nickel and titanium — the most widely used SMA. Used in spectacle frames, dental braces and medical stents.
A thermoforming polymer that softens at about 62°C in hot water, is moulded by hand and can be reshaped many times.
A polymer that conducts electricity — used in flexible circuits, touch surfaces, anti-static packaging and wearables.
A fingerprint cannot be changed if it is stolen, so data storage must be secure and the system must work for all users.
Absorbs heat as it melts and releases it as it solidifies, holding a temperature steady — clothing, bedding, cool packs.
Two or more materials combined for better properties, usually fibres for strength in a matrix such as resin.
Carbon fibres in epoxy resin. Extremely strong and stiff for its weight but very expensive — racing bikes, F1 cars, aircraft.
Glass fibres in polyester resin. Strong, light, waterproof, moulds into large shapes, cheaper than carbon fibre — boat hulls, car panels.
The common name for GRP, and for the glass fibres themselves, which are also used as loft insulation.
Laying fibre mat or cloth into a mould and brushing or rolling in resin with a hardener or catalyst, which cures into a rigid shell.
Short-range (about 10 m), low-power wireless technology connecting devices directly, e.g. earbuds to a phone.
Wireless technology connecting devices to a local network and the internet through a router — longer range and faster than Bluetooth.
Everyday products with sensors, processors and wireless connections that collect data, communicate and can be controlled remotely.
Remote control, products that adapt, energy saving, useful data — but hacking, privacy concerns, obsolescence if support ends, cost and e-waste.
A type of AI in which software improves at a task by finding patterns in large amounts of data, rather than following fixed instructions.

front: How AI is used in product development
back: Generative design, predicting performance, analysing user data, smarter products (voice assistants, robot vacuums) and inspecting products on production lines.

front: Emerging technology as a driving force
back: Technology push — new components, materials, processes and connectivity make new products possible, e.g. tiny sensors enabling fitness trackers.
